A rejection must be explainable.

`reason` is required: a clip rejected with no stated reason cannot be acted on by whoever
re-renders it, so the API refuses the request rather than storing a blank refusal.

get.description:
Caption cues for this clip window, rebuilt from the stored word timings.

Rebuilding rather than reading a cached file means the response is always consistent with the
transcript that exists now, and the coverage numbers are computed from real data instead of
being asserted. `words_without_timing` is reported, not hidden.

Where the rendered file lives.

The local storage backend cannot mint a signed URL and does not pretend to; it returns the
storage key so the caller knows exactly what exists. A real URL only appears once an
S3-compatible backend is configured.

post.description:
Refuse a rendered clip, with a reason, and allow it to be rendered again.

Rejecting is the only way a reviewed clip becomes re-renderable. That is deliberate: an
approved or simply unreviewed file is never overwritten, so the version a person judged is
always still there afterwards.

Cut, reframe and caption one clip into a new immutable version.

Runs in-request today (the render is bounded and seconds-long for short clips). The job row is
still written, so progress and failure are inspectable through `GET /jobs`.

post.description:
Mark an unfinished job cancelled.

This stops the *record* from being picked up or retried. It cannot interrupt a task already
executing inside a worker process — a CPU-bound FFmpeg or ASR call is not preemptible from
here, and pretending otherwise would be a lie. A running task that finishes will overwrite
this status on its own exit path.

post.description:
Queue audio extraction → transcription → candidate detection → scoring.

The work runs in a Celery worker, not in this request. The response is the *current* analysis
status: `status` reflects the project's stage, and `job_id` identifies the queued job so the
caller can poll `GET /jobs/{job_id}` for progress.

If an identical successful run already exists, nothing is queued and the existing result is
reported immediately (`reused=true`) — polling a finished analysis should never be a way to
accidentally pay for it twice.

Turn the selected candidate moments into clips. Does not render them.

Cheap and idempotent: calling it twice creates no duplicates, so it is safe to retry. Rendering
is a separate, explicit step because it costs minutes of CPU per clip.

post.description:
Upload a source video.

Order of checks: CSRF → workspace membership → rights declaration → extension/MIME/magic
bytes → real `ffprobe` inspection. The file is spooled to a temp file (bounded by
`MAX_UPLOAD_MB`), validated, then streamed into storage, so memory use stays constant.
On any rejection the stored object is removed — no orphaned bytes, no half-ingested project.
